catalogue.name: Money Plant
catalogue.note: The plant to fail on first, because you almost can't. Grows in a bottle of water on your desk.

catalogue.name: Neon Money Plant
catalogue.note: Acid-green leaves that glow in a dim corner. Same care as ordinary pothos.

catalogue.name: Marble Queen Pothos
catalogue.note: White-splashed. Loses variegation in deep shade, so keep it near the glass.

catalogue.name: Snake Plant
catalogue.note: Tolerates lower light than anything else sold in India. Easiest leaf to wipe dust off.

catalogue.name: Snake Plant 'Moonshine'
catalogue.note: Pale silver-green blades. A quiet upgrade on the ordinary snake plant.

catalogue.name: Mikado Snake Plant
catalogue.note: Thin cylindrical spears. Sculptural, and cheap for how good it looks.

catalogue.name: Dwarf Snake 'Hahnii'
catalogue.note: Compact rosette, right scale for a desk beside your monitor.

catalogue.name: Whale Fin Sansevieria
catalogue.note: One enormous paddle leaf. A specimen plant that asks nothing of you.

catalogue.name: ZZ Plant
catalogue.note: Most shade-tolerant houseplant sold in India. Rhizomes store water, so forgetting it is fine.

catalogue.name: Raven ZZ
catalogue.note: New growth emerges green then turns near-black. Slow, expensive, worth it.

catalogue.name: Heartleaf Philodendron
catalogue.note: Trails or climbs, roots from any cutting in water. Very hard to kill.

catalogue.name: Philodendron Birkin
catalogue.note: White pinstripes on deep green, every leaf patterned differently.

catalogue.name: Syngonium
catalogue.note: Fast, forgiving, comes in pink, cream and lime forms.

catalogue.name: Pink Syngonium 'Neon'
catalogue.note: Bubblegum-pink leaves that hold colour even in shade.

catalogue.name: Aglaonema
catalogue.note: Genuinely prefers shade. Pink-veined cultivars are the best colour you'll get without sun.

catalogue.name: Aglaonema 'Silver Bay'
catalogue.note: Broad silver-centred leaves, tolerant of neglect and dim corners.

catalogue.name: Peperomia
catalogue.note: You have one and it's thriving. Thick leaves store water, so it forgives missed weeks.

catalogue.name: Watermelon Peperomia
catalogue.note: Striped leaves that really do look like watermelon rind. Keep out of direct sun.

catalogue.name: Raindrop Peperomia
catalogue.note: Fat teardrop leaves. Often mistaken for Chinese money plant, easier to keep.

catalogue.name: Spider Plant
catalogue.note: You have the variegated form. Free plants forever from the runners.

catalogue.name: Nerve Plant
catalogue.note: Wants shade and humidity. In dry Talcher air it needs a pebble tray. Wilts dramatically, recovers in an hour.

catalogue.name: Boston Fern
catalogue.note: Easy in monsoon, needs daily misting March to May when humidity drops near 50%.

catalogue.name: Bird's Nest Fern
catalogue.note: Glossy unfurling fronds. Water into the soil, never into the central rosette.

catalogue.name: Peace Lily
catalogue.note: One of very few things that flowers in real shade. Droops theatrically when thirsty.

catalogue.name: Lucky Bamboo
catalogue.note: You have this. Keep it out of direct sun and change the water weekly.

catalogue.name: Cast Iron Plant
catalogue.note: Named for what it survives. Handles the darkest corner of the room.

catalogue.name: Chinese Money Plant
catalogue.note: Round coin leaves on thin stalks. Throws off pups you can pot separately.

catalogue.name: Silver Satin Pothos
catalogue.note: Matte leaves flecked with silver. Slower than pothos, better looking.

catalogue.name: Mini Monstera
catalogue.note: Split leaves on a compact climber. Give it a moss pole and it goes fast.

catalogue.name: Monstera adansonii
catalogue.note: Swiss-cheese holes. Trails beautifully from an upper shelf.

catalogue.name: Monstera
catalogue.note: Gets big. Needs floor space in a few years, but tolerates shade throughout.

catalogue.name: Prayer Plant
catalogue.note: Folds its leaves upward at night. Hates hard tap water — use stored or filtered.

catalogue.name: Calathea Orbifolia
catalogue.note: Spectacular silver banding and genuinely fussy. Hard in dry inland air.

catalogue.name: Song of India
catalogue.note: Yellow-margined spirals of foliage. Slow, sturdy, tolerant.

catalogue.name: Areca Palm
catalogue.note: Cheap, big, and softens a hard concrete room instantly.

catalogue.name: Anthurium
catalogue.note: Waxy red or pink spathes lasting weeks. Flowers in bright shade.

catalogue.name: Alocasia 'Black Velvet'
catalogue.note: Matte black leaves, white veins. Goes dormant when cold — don't panic in January.

catalogue.name: Alocasia 'Frydek'
catalogue.note: Velvet green arrowheads. Spider-mite magnet in your dry season.

catalogue.name: Polka Dot Begonia
catalogue.note: Silver-spotted wings over red undersides. Wants humidity and airflow at once.

catalogue.name: Wax Plant
catalogue.note: Waxy trailing vine, eventually clusters of scented star flowers. Very drought tolerant.

catalogue.name: Sweetheart Hoya
catalogue.note: A single heart-shaped leaf. Buy the version with a stem if you want it to grow.

catalogue.name: Wandering Jew
catalogue.note: Purple and silver stripes, roots from any snapped stem. Colours deepen with light.

catalogue.name: Tradescantia 'Nanouk'
catalogue.note: Chunky pink and cream stripes. Pinch it back or it goes leggy.

catalogue.name: Purple Shamrock
catalogue.note: Deep purple butterfly leaves that fold at night. Dies back and returns.

catalogue.name: Moon Valley Pilea
catalogue.note: Deeply quilted lime leaves. Compact enough for a desk.

catalogue.name: Zebra Haworthia
catalogue.note: The one succulent that copes with less light. White banding, tight rosette, very slow.

catalogue.name: Cooper's Haworthia
catalogue.note: Translucent windowed leaves that light passes straight through. Best succulent for shade.

catalogue.name: Zebra Wart
catalogue.note: Towers of white-warted leaves. Often thrown in free as a bundle bonus.

catalogue.name: Jade Plant
catalogue.note: You have one. Thickens into a small tree over years. Water deeply, then leave it alone.

catalogue.name: Gollum Jade
catalogue.note: Tubular leaves with red suction-cup tips. Same easy care as ordinary jade.

catalogue.name: Elephant Bush
catalogue.note: Grows fast, roots from cuttings, leaves are edible and lemony.

catalogue.name: Variegated Elephant Bush
catalogue.note: Cream-edged and pink-stemmed. Slower than the green form, twice as pretty.

catalogue.name: Echeveria
catalogue.note: The classic rosette. Stretches pale without real light — front row or under the lamp.

catalogue.name: Echeveria 'Black Prince'
catalogue.note: Near-black rosettes that only darken with strong light.

catalogue.name: Laxmi Kamal
catalogue.note: Cheapest good-looking succulent on the market. Produces offsets constantly.

catalogue.name: Jelly Bean Sedum
catalogue.note: Green beans that turn scarlet in sun. Dropped leaves root themselves everywhere.

catalogue.name: Sedum 'Tokyo Sun'
catalogue.note: Mat of tiny golden beads. Reverts to plain green without light.

catalogue.name: Graptoveria
catalogue.note: Pastel rosettes, tougher than they look. Good first pretty succulent.

catalogue.name: Kalanchoe millotii
catalogue.note: Soft grey felted leaves with scalloped edges. Handles humidity better than most.

catalogue.name: Flowering Kalanchoe
catalogue.note: Dense clusters of tiny flowers through winter. Treat as seasonal colour.

catalogue.name: String of Banana
catalogue.note: Trailing curved beads. Considerably more forgiving than string of pearls.

catalogue.name: String of Pearls
catalogue.note: Beautiful, and it rots the moment humidity climbs. Your dry March–May is its best window.

catalogue.name: Tiger Tooth Aloe
catalogue.note: Toothy stacked rosettes that turn bronze in strong light.

catalogue.name: Aloe Vera
catalogue.note: Useful and nearly indestructible. Needs light to stay compact rather than floppy.

catalogue.name: Gasteria
catalogue.note: Tongue-shaped speckled leaves, tolerant of lower light than most succulents.

catalogue.name: Panda Plant
catalogue.note: Fuzzy silver leaves with chocolate edges. Don't wet the fur.

catalogue.name: Mixed Mini Cactus
catalogue.note: Cheap, tiny, and the safest cactus purchase is a winter one when transit is dry.

catalogue.name: Bunny Ear Cactus
catalogue.note: Pads covered in golden glochids. Handle with tongs — those hairs are misery.

catalogue.name: Golden Barrel Cactus
catalogue.note: Perfect ribbed golden sphere. Extremely slow, effectively permanent.

catalogue.name: Moon Cactus
catalogue.note: The neon ball grafted onto a green stem. Colourful, short-lived, cheap.

catalogue.name: Coral Cactus
catalogue.note: Grafted fan-shaped crest. Not a cactus, and the milky sap burns skin and eyes.

catalogue.name: Lithops
catalogue.note: Kill more beginners than anything else. A wishlist item, not a starter.

catalogue.name: Desert Rose (seedling)
catalogue.note: Fat caudex, flower colour a lottery, blooms in year one or two. The sensible first adenium.

catalogue.name: Desert Rose (grafted)
catalogue.note: Known flower colour and flowers sooner, slimmer caudex. Buy after a seedling survives a year.

catalogue.name: Adenium arabicum
catalogue.note: Grown for the enormous squat caudex rather than the flowers.

catalogue.name: Madagascar Palm
catalogue.note: Spiny silver trunk with a crown of leaves. Wants the brightest spot you have.

catalogue.name: Stephania erecta
catalogue.note: Arrives as a bare brown bulb that sprouts a delicate umbrella vine. Quietly spectacular.

catalogue.name: Sago Palm
catalogue.note: A living fossil, stiff and architectural. Very slow.

catalogue.name: Elephant's Foot
catalogue.note: Cracked tortoiseshell caudex with a seasonal vine. Respect the dormancy.

catalogue.name: Pitcher Plant
catalogue.note: Hanging pitchers that catch your fungus gnats. Warm, humid, bright shade.

catalogue.name: Cape Sundew
catalogue.note: Dewy tentacles that curl around insects. Easiest carnivore to start with. Rainwater only.

catalogue.name: Trumpet Pitcher
catalogue.note: Tall upright trumpets. Needs strong light and a real winter dormancy.

catalogue.name: Venus Flytrap
catalogue.note: Everyone wants one. Distilled water only and a cold rest. Your May heat is the killer.

catalogue.name: Moth Orchid
catalogue.note: The one orchid built for a shaded spot. Flowers for months. Grow in bark, never soil.

catalogue.name: Dendrobium Orchid
catalogue.note: Canes of flowers, well suited to Odisha heat. Likes to dry between waterings.

catalogue.name: Vanda Orchid
catalogue.note: Grown hanging with bare roots, no pot at all. Bright light and daily water.

catalogue.name: Dancing Lady Orchid
catalogue.note: Sprays of small yellow flowers. Fussier about water quality than dendrobium.

catalogue.name: Ficus Ginseng bonsai
catalogue.note: The beginner bonsai. Swollen aerial roots, tolerates shade, forgives bad pruning.

catalogue.name: Peepal bonsai
catalogue.note: Native, thrives in Odisha heat, grows fast enough that mistakes grow out in a season.

catalogue.name: Weeping Fig bonsai
catalogue.note: Fine leaves and elegant branching. Drops leaves when moved — that is normal.

catalogue.name: Money Tree bonsai
catalogue.note: Braided trunk, handles low light better than any other bonsai subject.

catalogue.name: Fukien Tea bonsai
catalogue.note: Tiny glossy leaves and small white flowers. Needs real light — front row only.

catalogue.name: Umbrella Tree bonsai
catalogue.note: Very shade-tolerant, grows aerial roots readily. A good second bonsai.

catalogue.name: Chinese Elm bonsai
catalogue.note: Classic fine ramification and the best species to learn actual styling on.

catalogue.name: Bougainvillea bonsai
catalogue.note: Blazing colour, but needs six hours of light to flower. Front row or nothing.

catalogue.name: Adenium bonsai
catalogue.note: Caudex styled as bonsai — combines the two things you're interested in.

catalogue.name: Serissa bonsai
catalogue.note: Tiny white flowers, and famously sulky — drops every leaf if you move it.

catalogue.name: Bird's Eye Chilli
catalogue.note: The most realistic fruiting plant for a low-light room. Grows from kitchen seed.

catalogue.name: Cherry Tomato
catalogue.note: Sow October, harvest December to February. Summer heat stops fruit setting entirely.

catalogue.name: Kagzi Lime
catalogue.note: Compact, fragrant, genuinely productive if it gets the front row.

catalogue.name: Kaffir Lime
catalogue.note: Grown for the double leaves rather than the fruit. Worth it for the kitchen alone.

catalogue.name: Dwarf Pomegranate
catalogue.note: Small orange flowers and miniature fruit. Made for containers, loves your dry heat.

catalogue.name: Dwarf Guava L-49
catalogue.note: Grafted dwarf that fruits in a pot within two years. Perfectly suited to Odisha.

catalogue.name: Barbados Cherry
catalogue.note: Extraordinary vitamin C, fruits several times a year, stays small in a pot.

catalogue.name: Karonda
catalogue.note: Tough native shrub, thorny, fruits reliably. Handles 45°C without blinking.

catalogue.name: Fig 'Brown Turkey'
catalogue.note: One of the few fruit trees that genuinely performs in a container.

catalogue.name: Dwarf Banana
catalogue.note: Big tropical leaves and it will fruit in a large pot. Wants constant water and feeding.

catalogue.name: Strawberry
catalogue.note: Plant November, harvest February. A winter-only crop, but your cool January suits it.

catalogue.name: Passion Fruit
catalogue.note: Vigorous vine with extraordinary flowers. Give it the window and something to climb.

catalogue.name: Dwarf Mango Amrapali
catalogue.note: A real mango in a pot. Slow, demanding, a genuine project rather than a plant.

catalogue.name: Black Mulberry
catalogue.note: Fruits young, tolerates pot life, grows fast from a cutting.

catalogue.name: Mint / Podina
catalogue.note: Grows in partial shade and spreads aggressively. Always give it its own pot.

catalogue.name: Ajwain Patta
catalogue.note: Thick aromatic leaves, thrives on neglect, roots from a snapped stem in water.

catalogue.name: Curry Leaf
catalogue.note: Wants light but limps along in bright shade. Endlessly useful in an Odia kitchen.

catalogue.name: Lemongrass
catalogue.note: Start it from a supermarket stalk stood in water. Costs nothing.

catalogue.name: Poi Saga
catalogue.note: A climbing green that prefers partial shade and monsoon heat. Local staple.

catalogue.name: Coriander / Dhania
catalogue.note: Sow October to January. It bolts within weeks once the heat returns.

catalogue.name: Tulasi
catalogue.note: Wants light but survives bright shade. Pinch flower spikes to keep leaves coming.

catalogue.name: Rosemary
catalogue.note: Hates humidity. Dry December to March is its one window; expect to lose it in monsoon.

catalogue.name: Haladi / Turmeric
catalogue.note: Grows from a rhizome, wants heat, water and light. Dies back completely around December and re-sprouts in spring — that is normal, keep the pot.

catalogue.name: Shell Ginger
catalogue.note: Pseudostem of rolled leaf sheaths, leaves in two ranks. Evergreen rather than dormant, but it gets big and will outgrow a small pot in a year.

catalogue.name: Amrapali mango
catalogue.note: The true dwarf, bred at IARI for high-density planting — which is exactly what a container is. Regular bearer, unlike most mangoes. Prune only Aug–Sep. Remove the first flowering to build a frame.

catalogue.name: Mallika mango
catalogue.note: Neelam × Dashehari, same cross as Amrapali. Bigger fruit, better keeping, semi-dwarf rather than dwarf. The one to add second.

catalogue.name: Dashehari mango
catalogue.note: Superb fruit, but a strong alternate bearer — heavy one year, nothing the next — and it gets large. Better in the ground than a bag.

catalogue.name: Kesar mango
catalogue.note: Gujarat variety, saffron flesh, excellent. Wants a drier flowering season than coastal Odisha reliably gives — expect anthracnose pressure at bloom.

catalogue.name: Arka Neelkiran mango
catalogue.note: IIHR hybrid, regular bearer, good anthracnose tolerance — which matters more here than flavour rankings. Portal or CHES only.

catalogue.name: Banganapalli mango
catalogue.note: The Andhra commercial standard, well adapted to your latitude and heat. Too vigorous for a bag — save it for the ground plot.

catalogue.name: Alphonso mango
catalogue.note: Ruled out, and not for heat. Alphonso needs the Konkan's laterite plus coastal humidity pattern; outside it, spongy tissue and severe alternate bearing are routine. Buy the fruit, not the tree.

catalogue.name: Red Diamond guava
catalogue.note: Red flesh, low seed, fruits within a year of layering. Fruits on new wood, so cutting back after each harvest is what creates the next crop. Most wilt-prone thing you can own — drainage decides it.

catalogue.name: Taiwan Pink guava
catalogue.note: The reliability benchmark. Heavier cropper than Red Diamond and less fussy. Grow both and let one season settle the argument.

catalogue.name: Allahabad Safeda guava
catalogue.note: White flesh, the Indian standard, and the toughest guava sold. Less exciting, more dependable.

catalogue.name: Arka Kiran guava
catalogue.note: IIHR red-flesh selection, high lycopene, bred for peninsular India. Portal only.

catalogue.name: Thai Seedless guava
catalogue.note: Genuinely seedless, but yields less and the plant is weaker. A novelty second, never a first guava.

catalogue.name: White jamun
catalogue.note: Uncommon, sweeter and less astringent than the black. Strong taproot, so height over width. Fruit drop is a watering-consistency problem, never a nutrient one.

catalogue.name: Konkan Bahadoli jamun
catalogue.note: A real named release from Dr BSKKV, unlike most jamun sold under invented names. Large fruit, small stone. Ask for it by name.

catalogue.name: Goma Priyanka jamun
catalogue.note: CHES Godhra release, bred for arid and semi-arid heat. The best-documented jamun available to you.

catalogue.name: Kalipatti sapota
catalogue.note: The Maharashtra commercial standard. Will look like it is doing nothing for three years — that is normal, and the commonest way a container sapota dies is an owner reading slow growth as hunger.

catalogue.name: Cricket Ball sapota
catalogue.note: Very large fruit, coarser texture, bigger tree. Kalipatti is the better container choice.

catalogue.name: Kagzi lime
catalogue.note: The easiest citrus in India and near-everbearing in your climate. 30% shade Mar–Jun. Watch pH — above 7.5 the leaves go yellow between green veins and more fertiliser will not help.

catalogue.name: Kaffir lime
catalogue.note: Grown for the leaf, not the fruit, so it crops from year one. Wants 40% shade year-round here. Leaf miner is the constant enemy.

catalogue.name: Nagpur mandarin
catalogue.note: Needs a distinct cool dry spell to sweeten, and coastal Odisha barely gives one — expect fruit that colours but stays sour. Citrus greening is endemic; buy only certified stock.

catalogue.name: Finger lime
catalogue.note: Expensive, slow, thorny, and needs 40–50% shade permanently. Genuinely unusual fruit. Buy it when the rest of the collection is stable, not before.

catalogue.name: Red Lady 786 papaya
catalogue.note: Gynodioecious, so one plant fruits alone. Single stem, never prune, mound-plant. Collar rot in monsoon is what kills it. Three-year life, then replace rather than nurse.

catalogue.name: Dragon fruit, red flesh
catalogue.note: A cactus, so the terrace suits it perfectly. Fruits in 12–18 months from a cutting. Most red-flesh types need cross-pollination — buy two clones, and hand-pollinate at night with a brush.

catalogue.name: Dragon fruit, white flesh
catalogue.note: Mostly self-fertile, unlike the red. Less flavour, far fewer problems. Start here.

catalogue.name: Thai apple ber
catalogue.note: Fruits the first winter after planting — the fastest tree fruit you can buy. Thrives on heat and neglect. Cut it back hard every year after harvest or it becomes a thicket.

catalogue.name: Bhagwa pomegranate
catalogue.note: Fruits well, but pomegranate hates humidity at ripening — expect fruit cracking and bacterial blight through the monsoon. Best if you can shelter it Jul–Sep.

catalogue.name: Fig, Brown Turkey / Poona
catalogue.note: Roots from a cutting in weeks, so it costs nothing to multiply. Common types need no pollinator. Ripening fruit splits in direct monsoon rain — it needs the balcony, not the open.

catalogue.name: Grand Naine banana
catalogue.note: Fast and reliable, but a heavy feeder and a heavy drinker, and it topples in terrace wind. Ground plot only. Buy tissue culture, never a random sucker — that is how Panama disease arrives.

catalogue.name: MD-2 pineapple
catalogue.note: A bromeliad — shallow-rooted, drought-tolerant, ideal for a hot terrace. Force flowering at 12 months with ethylene (a ripe apple in a bag over the plant for three days) rather than waiting.

catalogue.name: Passion fruit, purple
catalogue.note: Fast and heavy-bearing, but short-lived here — three or four years before Fusarium takes it. Plan to replace rather than to keep.

catalogue.name: Barbados cherry
catalogue.note: Three or four crops a year, extraordinary vitamin C, and it genuinely prefers 40% shade — which makes it the best plant for Zone D.

catalogue.name: Karonda
catalogue.note: Native, thorny, effectively indestructible, and it fruits through the worst of the heat. The plant to own if you want something that cannot be killed.

catalogue.name: Phalsa
catalogue.note: Fruits on new wood, so cut it to a metre each January. Ripens in May, when nothing else does — which is the whole argument for it.

catalogue.name: Mulberry, dwarf black
catalogue.note: Roots from a cutting almost without trying and fruits the first year. Prune hard and often. The cheapest fast win on this list after the ber.

catalogue.name: Custard apple, Arka Sahan
catalogue.note: IIHR hybrid, large fruit, few seeds. Deciduous — it drops its leaves in winter and looks dead. Do not throw it out. Hand-pollinate at dusk for real yields.

catalogue.name: Jackfruit, dwarf (Vietnam Super Early)
catalogue.note: Grafted dwarf types fruit in two years at chest height. Seedling jackfruit is a 15 m forest tree at eight years — the difference is entirely in the propagation, so verify the graft union.

catalogue.name: Jaboticaba
catalogue.note: Fruit straight off the trunk, and worth owning. But it is acid-loving, hates alkaline water, and a seedling will outlive your patience. Grafted only, and check pH monthly.

catalogue.name: Abiu
catalogue.note: Amazonian, needs shade while young and real humidity. Your May is its worst month. A Zone D plant with fogger support, or not at all.

catalogue.name: Miracle fruit
catalogue.note: Demands acid mix at pH 4.5–5.5 and will decline slowly in ordinary water. A project plant, not a fruit crop. Rainwater only.

catalogue.name: Star fruit / Carambola
catalogue.note: Two or three crops a year and genuinely easy. Wants 30% shade Mar–Jun and constant moisture — it drops fruit at the first dry spell.

catalogue.name: Water apple / Jamrul
catalogue.note: Perfect for a humid coastal climate and heavy-bearing once established. Fruit is mostly water — grow it for the volume and the shade, not the flavour.

catalogue.name: Bael
catalogue.note: Native, sacred, and thrives on exactly the heat and neglect that kills everything else. Grafted types fruit in three years; seedlings take eight.

catalogue.name: Avocado, grafted
catalogue.note: Ruled out for a bag. Avocado dies of root rot in any container that holds water, and coastal Odisha's monsoon guarantees it. A ground plot with a raised mound is the only version that works.

catalogue.name: Apple
catalogue.note: Ruled out on chill hours, not heat. Apple needs 800–1200 hours below 7°C to break dormancy; Talcher gets effectively zero. It will leaf out raggedly and never flower. Kadiyam sells "Kashmiri apple" grafts anyway — do not buy one.

catalogue.name: Litchi
catalogue.note: Needs a cool dry November–December to initiate flowering, and a huge undisturbed root run. It will grow here and never fruit. The single most commonly mis-sold tree in eastern India.

catalogue.name: Peach, plum, apricot, cherry
catalogue.note: Same chill problem as apple. Low-chill peach cultivars exist (Florida Prince, Shan-e-Punjab at ~150 hours) but even those need more cold than you get.

catalogue.name: Mangosteen
catalogue.note: Fails on your dry gap, not your heat. Mangosteen needs year-round humidity above 70% and no dry season at all — Kerala and the Andamans, not Angul. Ten years to fruit even where it works.

catalogue.name: Rambutan, durian
catalogue.note: Equatorial species with no dry-season tolerance. March to June at 15% humidity kills them outright.

catalogue.name: Grafted brinjal
catalogue.note: The union must stay 2–3 inches above soil forever, or the wilt resistance you paid for is wasted. Ratoon to one foot after each flush and feed hard.

catalogue.name: Grafted chilli
catalogue.note: Same union rule. Thrips-borne leaf curl is what ends chillies here — blue sticky trap from day one, not after you see damage.

catalogue.name: Roselle / Gongura
catalogue.note: Leaves from six weeks, calyces in November. Thrives in exactly the heat that stops everything else.

catalogue.name: Cape gooseberry
catalogue.note: Fruits in a single season from seed, self-fertile, and it likes the balcony. One of the few things that will actually crop in your first winter.

catalogue.name: Radish Pusa Chetki (seed)
catalogue.note: A genuine IARI variety, heat-tolerant, roots in 40 days. Best-value seed in the whole sheet. Sow: Direct. 8–10 roots per bag.
catalogue.cyc: 40–45 days · One-shot. Re-sow every 2 weeks, Oct–Jan

catalogue.name: Lettuce Biscia Salad Bowl Red (seed)
catalogue.note: Loose-leaf. You harvest leaves for months instead of one head once — which is why it beats iceberg in a pot. Sow: Direct or transplant. 3–4 per bag.

catalogue.name: Lettuce Lollo Rosso (seed)
catalogue.note: Same habit, red frilled, holds up better as the balcony warms. Sow: Direct. 3–4 per bag.

catalogue.name: Early Coriander (seed)
catalogue.note: A thousand seeds means a fresh tray every two weeks all winter. Sow: Direct. Broadcast per bag.

catalogue.name: Spinach / Palak (seed)
catalogue.note: The bulk leafy crop for Zone C. Untreated OP version also exists at ₹69. Sow: Direct. Broadcast per bag.

catalogue.name: Fenugreek / Methi (seed)
catalogue.note: Three weeks from seed to harvest. The cheapest greens you can grow. Sow: Direct. Dense broadcast per bag.

catalogue.name: Capsicum California Wonder (seed)
catalogue.note: The reliable open-pollinated bell pepper standard. Save your own seed from it. Sow: Tray → transplant. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Capsicum Orange (OP) (seed)
catalogue.note: Open-pollinated, so seed-saving works. Half the price of the F1 colour packets. Sow: Tray → transplant. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Chilli Jwala (seed)
catalogue.note: Named, proven Indian variety. High yield in a 14-inch bag. Sow: Tray → transplant. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Bird's Eye / Kanthari chilli (seed)
catalogue.note: Exactly the local Kanthari the plan called for. Hard cut-back each March and it keeps cropping. Sow: Tray → transplant at 30–35 d. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Seeni Milagai — short bird's eye (seed)
catalogue.note: Short-statured bird's eye. A better pot plant than the tall type. Sow: Tray → transplant. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Carrot Early Nantes (seed)
catalogue.note: Nantes is the short blunt type — the only carrot shape that works in a 12-inch bag. Sow: Direct. 15–20 roots per bag.

catalogue.name: Beetroot, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: Open-pollinated, so seed-saving works. Sow: Direct. 8–10 per bag.

catalogue.name: Spring onion, bunching (seed)
catalogue.note: Skip bulb onion — five months to a bulb is poor value per litre of pot. Sow: Direct. Dense per bag.

catalogue.name: Red Amaranth — lal bhaji (seed)
catalogue.note: Five grams is thousands of seeds. Arka Arunima is not available here; this is the working substitute. Sow: Direct. Broadcast 15–20 per bag.

catalogue.name: Chaulai Green — hari bhaji (seed)
catalogue.note: Faster regrowth than the red. Sow: Direct. Broadcast per bag.

catalogue.name: Amaranthus Red / Green (seed)
catalogue.note: The same crop at a third of the price if you do not need the bigger pack. Sow: Direct. Broadcast per bag.

catalogue.name: Okra Pusa Sawni (seed)
catalogue.note: A genuine IARI variety, available without the Delhi trip. See the upgrade note — it is not YVMV-resistant. Sow: Direct — taproot, hates transplant. 1 per bag.
catalogue.cyc: 45–50 days · Pick every 2 days for 60–75 days

catalogue.name: Okra Varsha (seed)
catalogue.note: Monsoon-season type. A useful second string. Sow: Direct. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Red Okra — lal bhindi (seed)
catalogue.note: Genuinely different, sells well, identical culture. Sow: Direct. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: French Beans Bush Type (Dwarf) (seed)
catalogue.note: The only bean listing that states dwarf habit outright. Everything else is a guess. Sow: Direct — never transplant. 3–4 per bag.
catalogue.cyc: 45–55 days · 3–4 weeks, then pull. Sow Oct and Feb

catalogue.name: Cowpea / Lobia (seed)
catalogue.note: Habit is not stated — could be bush or pole. Give it a stake and find out. Sow: Direct. 3–4 per bag.

catalogue.name: Gongura / Roselle (seed)
catalogue.note: The only roselle in 8,165 rows, and it costs fifteen rupees. Sow: Direct, June. 1 per bag.
catalogue.cyc: Leaves 45–60 d; calyces Nov–Dec · 6–8 month plant

catalogue.name: Radish White Long, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: Open-pollinated and untreated. Save seed and never buy again. Sow: Direct. 8–10 per bag.

catalogue.name: Chilli, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: OP. The cheapest entry into the seed-saving line. Sow: Tray. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Cherry Tomato, untreated OP (seed)
catalogue.note: Bag a truss in muslin before it opens and save seed only from that. Sow: Tray. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Tomato, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: OP salad tomato. Sow: Tray. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Okra, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Direct. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Beetroot, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Direct. 8–10 per bag.

catalogue.name: Broccoli, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Tray. 1–2 per bag.

catalogue.name: Cabbage, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Tray. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Cauliflower, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Tray. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Carrot Orange, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Direct. 15–20 per bag.

catalogue.name: Coriander, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Direct. Broadcast per bag.

catalogue.name: Spinach, untreated (seed)
catalogue.note: All twelve untreated crops together come to ₹610 — a complete self-renewing garden. Sow: Direct. Broadcast per bag.

catalogue.name: Krishna / Shyam Basil (seed)
catalogue.note: Cheapest herb seed in the sheet. Sow: Tray or direct. 1–2 per bag.

catalogue.name: Italian Large Leaf Basil (seed)
catalogue.note: Plant one beside each tomato. Real whitefly deterrence, not folklore. Sow: Tray. 1–2 per bag.

catalogue.name: Lemon Basil (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Direct. 1–2 per bag.

catalogue.name: Oregano (seed)
catalogue.note: Slow from seed but permanent once it is up. Sow: Tray, surface-sown. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Thyme (seed)
catalogue.note: Zone C. Hates monsoon wet — keep it under cover July to September. Sow: Tray. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Parsley (seed)
catalogue.note: Germinates in three weeks. Do not give up on it early — most people do. Sow: Direct. 2–3 per bag.

catalogue.name: Chives, medium leaf (seed)
catalogue.note: Zone D. Cut and it regrows indefinitely. Sow: Direct. Clump per bag.

catalogue.name: Fenugreek Microgreens (seed)
catalogue.note: Best value per gram in the entire sheet. This is what you grow in May, when nothing outdoors is producing. Sow: Direct, no cover. Dense broadcast per bag.
catalogue.cyc: 7–10 days · Single cut · ~5 trays per pack

catalogue.name: Radish Microgreens (seed)
catalogue.note: Peppery. The fastest of the lot. Sow: Direct. Dense per bag.

catalogue.name: Sunflower Microgreens (seed)
catalogue.note: Highest biomass by weight of any microgreen here. Sow: Soak 8 h first. Dense per bag.

catalogue.name: Spinach Microgreens (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Direct. Dense per bag.

catalogue.name: Coriander Microgreens (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Direct. Dense per bag.

catalogue.name: Red Amaranth Microgreens (seed)
catalogue.note: Best-looking of the lot. Sow: Direct. Dense per bag.

catalogue.name: Beetroot Microgreens (seed)
catalogue.note: — Sow: Soak first. Dense per bag.

catalogue.name: Marigold Pusa Navrangi (seed)
catalogue.size: 8×8, or interplant into a fruiting bag
catalogue.note: A genuine IARI variety. Root exudates suppress nematodes — plant one in each brinjal and tomato bag. Not decoration. Sow: Tray → transplant. 1 per bag.
catalogue.bagf: 8×8, or interplant into a fruiting bag

catalogue.name: French Marigold Scarlet Red (seed)
catalogue.note: Tagetes patula has the stronger nematode evidence than the African types. Pair it with the Pusa. Sow: Tray. 1 per bag.

catalogue.name: Cape Gooseberry — Rasbhari (seed)
catalogue.note: The only source in the sheet, and it fruits in a single season. Zone C. Sow: Tray → transplant. 1 per bag.
